2026-07-23-forecast-uncertainty-expansio.title: How to Read a Forecast Range
2026-07-23-forecast-uncertainty-expansio.description: Use forecast quantiles to compare possible outcomes and understand what a median leaves out.
2026-07-23-forecast-uncertainty-expansio.body:
A forecast is a set of estimates made from a particular history, model configuration, and cutoff. The median is useful, but the surrounding range helps you ask better questions about uncertainty.

Start with the median, then widen your view

P50 is the model's median estimate at each forecast timestamp. P25 and P75 describe the middle of its predicted distribution; P01 and P99 describe more extreme estimates. These are model quantiles. Their labels do not prove that future prices will fall inside the range at the stated rate.

Compare the same timestamp

Match the observed price to the forecast date and horizon you are reviewing. A terminal P50 seven days ahead answers a different question from tomorrow's P50. A range that widens over time indicates increasing model uncertainty; it does not establish that a trade has an edge.

Check which models support the range

Inspect the models and effective weights. A model may support central quantiles while another supplies the extreme tails. Quantura's game ensembles exclude models without native P01/P99 support from those tail calculations.

Turn the output into a research question

Write down the outcome you want to test, the forecast cutoff, and the evidence that would change your view. Save the result before reviewing later observations. Compare several forecasts with realized outcomes; avoid drawing a conclusion from one successful example.

Explore a forecast

2025-10-02-data-freshness-slas-for-forec.title: Check the Data Behind Your Forecast
2025-10-02-data-freshness-slas-for-forec.description: A practical checklist for source identity, observation cutoffs, missing data, and model coverage.
2025-10-02-data-freshness-slas-for-forec.body:
A useful forecast begins with a dataset you can explain. Before interpreting the chart, check what was observed, when it became available, and how it reached the model.

Verify the source and instrument

An exchange stock, a CFD, and a prediction-market contract are different instruments. Check the provider and symbol. For Dukascopy quotes, retain the selected bid or ask side and the published price scale. Changing a provider can change the meaning of a series.

Read the cutoff

The last completed observation tells you what information was available to the forecast. A candle's start time differs from the time its closing price becomes available. Historical strategy research must also account for the time needed to produce the forecast.

Keep missing observations visible

Check observation counts and gaps. Weekends, market closures, and periods without genuine observations are not interchangeable with feed failures. Filling a gap introduces an assumption; silently filling it makes the output harder to interpret.

Separate a forecast from evidence of accuracy

Record the models, quantiles, and horizon. Then compare saved estimates with later observations or a chronological holdout. Repeatedly choosing a rule after seeing the same outcomes can make a result look stronger than it is.

For a game, verify kickoff with the provider. A market's listing date or settlement deadline should not be treated as the start of play.

Review a forecast's context

2026-08-06-chronological-csv-exports-tha.title: From a Clean Time Series to Portable Research
2026-08-06-chronological-csv-exports-tha.description: Prepare a CSV, inspect a forecast, and preserve the timestamps and context needed to review it later.
2026-08-06-chronological-csv-exports-tha.body:
A spreadsheet should help you follow the research, not hide how it was produced. A clean time series and an explicit export make it easier to compare model estimates with later observations.

Make the input unambiguous

Use one timestamp column and one numeric target column. Sort timestamps, check duplicates, state the timezone, and verify the frequency. Price quotes and contract probabilities use different units. Keep the source and any adjustment choices with the file.

Choose a question and horizon

In Forecast, select your CSV columns, models, quantiles, and horizon. Inspect the observation count before running. A longer forecast or another model cannot repair missing or incorrectly labeled inputs.

Keep the output together

Save your forecast to Requests, then export the quantile table for a spreadsheet or another analysis tool. Preserve the source, input cutoff, model choices, and forecast timestamps alongside the predictions. Developers can use protected APIs when the same workflow needs to run in their own tools.

Review without changing the original question

Add realized observations in a separate column. Compare them at matching timestamps and record both useful forecasts and failures. Keep the original result so a later model refresh does not replace the evidence you intended to evaluate.
